extracted.intended_audience: researchers and graduate students in psychology, organizational behavior, and humor studies (scholars studying Benign Violation Theory, social distance, power, and culture)
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and evaluation criteria for when events/jokes are perceived as humorous under Benign Violation Theory, extended to include social distance, power asymmetry, and cultural context. Focuses on dyadic perspectives (joke-teller vs. joke-listener) and implications for research/design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign Violation (BVT) core criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Two simultaneous appraisals must be present for something to be regarded as funny: (1) the stimulus must represent a violation (contrary to expectations, threatening the person's view of how the world 'ought' to be), and (2) the violation must be perceived as benign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples range from playful physical violations (tickling) to linguistic norm violations. The BVT emphasises the necessity of both components together; if one is missing the stimulus will not be funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation (must be recognized as a threat to expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation is something contrary to expectations that threatens a person’s view of what the world 'ought' to be (can be physical, identity, cultural, communicative, linguistic, or logical norms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: being 'attacked' by a friend trying to tickle you, or violating a linguistic rule. A stimulus that is too harmless (no perceived threat) will not function as a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived benignness (violation must be seen as safe/harmless)
rubrics_metrics.description: The violation must be perceived as benign—i.e., 'safe, harmless, acceptable, nonserious, or okay'—for the stimulus to be humorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benignness may be influenced by psychological distance, attribution of intent, roles, culture, and social relationships. A violation judged as malign (offensive, threatening) will not be funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweet spot / distance range
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor occurs in a 'sweet spot' of psychological distance (temporal, geographical, hypothetical, or social) where a violation is close enough to be a violation but distant enough to be perceived as benign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too close (recent tragedy) or too far (too harmless/irrelevant) will reduce funniness. Empirical studies often look for this optimal range; the sweet spot differs across distance dimensions and individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological distance / construal level as determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological distance reduces the tendency to perceive events as threatening by promoting abstract construals; greater distance makes violations more likely to be seen as benign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distance operates along multiple dimensions and interacts with perceived severity; increased distance can make minor events less funny and serious events more funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four dimensions of psychological distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological distance comprises four dimensions that influence benignness: temporal distance (recent vs. long-ago), geographical distance (near vs. far), hypotheticality (actual vs. imagined), and social distance (self vs. others, familiar vs. unfamiliar, in-group vs. out-group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Much BVT research has focused on temporal and geographical distance; social and hypothetical distances require more study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish joke-teller vs. joke-listener perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: The model should explicitly distinguish the perspectives of the joke-teller and the joke-listener because their sweet spots and appraisals of violation/benignness may differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different roles, positions, and attributions of intent can produce disagreement within the same situation about whether something is a violation, benign, or funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social distance — listener-to-joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Social distance between the joke-listener and the joke: how socially close or committed the listener is to the persons/groups/roles/values implicated by the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the joke concerns an out-group or unfamiliar persons, violations may be more likely to be viewed as benign; identification with the target increases the chance the listener perceives the joke as malign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social distance — teller-to-joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived social distance between the joke-teller and the joke: whether the teller is socially close to or implicated in the content of the joke (influences attributions of intent, responsibility, and appropriateness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A teller perceived as close to the target (e.g., has personal ties) may be judged as having benign intent, making the violation more likely to be seen as benign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social distance — teller-to-listener
rubrics_metrics.description: Social distance between the joke-teller and the joke-listener: closeness of relationship, familiarity, in-group/out-group status, and differences in perceived distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater closeness often increases tolerance for role violations; unfamiliar or out-group tellers risk being perceived as malign, especially when combined with power differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative social distances (triadic relation of teller, joke, listener)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor appraisal depends on the relative distances among joke-teller, joke, and joke-listener—these three distances must be considered together rather than in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: same joke told by an in-group member vs. out-group member produces different appraisals; grandfather vs. millennial example illustrates inferred benign intent due to perceived distance to lingo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power differences influencing social distance and sweet spots
rubrics_metrics.description: Stable power asymmetries (hierarchical differences, social roles) predict social distance and thereby alter sweet spots: high-power individuals perceive greater social distance and more abstract construals than low-power individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power asymmetry can create mismatched sweet spots causing offensive/bland outcomes; power affects what counts as a violation and the impropriety threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impropriety threshold (power-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'impropriety threshold' marks when a violation is no longer perceived as benign. High-power individuals have higher impropriety thresholds (need more to see something as improper) than low-power individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teller is high-power and listener low-power, sweet-spot overlap may shrink or disappear—high-power tellers may overshoot and offend without realizing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathic inaccuracy in high-power individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: High-power persons are predicted to display empathic inaccuracy (reduced attention/responsiveness to others' mental states), which can make them less likely to detect that their attempted benign violations are perceived as malign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empathic inaccuracy increases risk of offensive jokes and contributes to vicious cycles of misjudged violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetric sweet spots / 'asymmetric upper' and 'asymmetric lower'
rubrics_metrics.description: When superimposing the sweet spots of teller and listener, nonoverlapping regions can arise: 'asymmetric upper' where teller sees benign violation but listener sees malign (offensive), and 'asymmetric lower' where teller sees benign violation but listener sees benign without perceiving it as a violation (bland).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conceptualization explains why the same joke can be offensive to some and bland or amusing to others within the same encounter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural influences on thresholds and power effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture affects humor via at least three mechanisms: (1) shifting absolute levels of what entire societies/organizations consider benign vs. malign, (2) influencing how power differences manifest and whether they produce asymmetric social distance, and (3) changing relative thresholds when teller and listener come from different cultural backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: national tightness-looseness, organizational norms (comedy club vs. workplace), Hofstede's power-distance dimension; culture also affects norms for expressing amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role violations and social expectations as sources of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of social roles, activities, tasks, and relationship expectations (e.g., teacher dancing on table, breaking doctor–patient confidentiality) can function as violations within BVT and be humorous if perceived as benign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Role ambiguity or breaking roles can be funny but may also have adverse consequences depending on context and power relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of intent and responsibility affects benignness
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptions about the teller's intent, responsibility, and relation to the target influence whether a violation is judged benign (e.g., perceived well-meaning intent increases likelihood of benign appraisal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research on attribution and responsibility (Weiner) implies that inferred intent can moderate humor perceptions strongly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention to amuse (scope limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The discussion and model focus on situations where humor is told with the explicit intention to amuse others; intentionally malicious uses of humor (bullying, power play) are conceptually distinct from attempts to hit the sweet spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses and predictions concern attempted benign violations rather than deliberately hurtful humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity of violation and nonlinearity (too harmless/too severe)
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation that is either too harmless (not a violation) or too severe (too threatening) will not be perceived as funny — funniness is nonmonotonic with severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: making a joke about a toe stub 5 years ago (too far/harmless) vs. being hit by a car yesterday (too close/severe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness norms for expressing amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural and situational norms influence whether individuals are expected or allowed to express amusement; these norms shape whether an event is publicly appraised as benign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations, societies, or subcultures may have shared impropriety thresholds and differing permissiveness for amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological criterion: level of analysis and inter-rater reliability expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Border-zone humor (near the sweet spot) requires dyadic or individual-level analysis because relative power and distance cause individual variation; group-level agreement and inter-rater reliability may be low in these zones but increase with severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should match analytic level to severity: dyadic/individual for border areas, group-level for clear benign/malign cases. Expect low inter-rater reliability in sweet-spot/border zones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectrum or 'border zone' behavior (humor as spectrum behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is characterized as spectrum behavior where the same behavior can be benign or malign depending on distance, power, culture, and other variables — unlike behaviors that are exclusively benign or malign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that humor can shift across the spectrum and that incremental changes (especially under power asymmetry) can lead to stepwise shifts toward malign violations (e.g., progressive boundary crossing).
